course.title: Applied Artificial Intelligence
course.shortDescription: Understand how machine learning actually works — classification, regression, neural networks, and clustering — and compute the metrics yourself in Python.
course.longDescription:
This showcase course follows the freeCodeCamp Machine Learning for Everybody curriculum by Kylie Ying, split into focused video segments with concept readings, scenario quizzes, and hands-on Python challenges where you implement the evaluation metrics — accuracy, mean squared error — that every ML engineer computes daily.

No prior ML experience needed; comfort with basic Python helps for the coding challenges. You will finish able to explain supervised vs. unsupervised learning, pick between classification models, describe how a neural network trains, and reason about model evaluation like a practitioner.
course.courseSummary: Features and labels, classification vs regression, train/validation/test splits, K-nearest neighbors, Naive Bayes, logistic regression, SVMs, neural networks and TensorFlow, linear regression, K-means clustering, PCA, and model evaluation metrics.

content.description: Features, labels, and the three flavors of machine learning — with a real dataset in Google Colab.
content.problemStatement: Features, labels, and the three flavors of machine learning — with a real dataset in Google Colab.

contentBlocks.content:
Programs that learn from examples

Classic software encodes rules by hand. Machine learning flips this: you supply examples (data) and the desired answers (labels), and the algorithm finds the rules itself. Three flavors matter:

  • Supervised learning — labeled examples; predict a label for new data (spam detection, medical diagnosis)
  • Unsupervised learning — no labels; find structure in the data (customer segmentation)
  • Reinforcement learning — an agent learns by trial, error, and reward (game-playing AI)

This segment introduces the vocabulary you will use for the rest of the course: features (the input columns), labels (the output to predict), and the difference between classification (predict a category) and regression (predict a number).

content.description: Train/validation/test splits, loss, and why data preparation decides whether your model works at all.
content.problemStatement: Train/validation/test splits, loss, and why data preparation decides whether your model works at all.

contentBlocks.content:
The golden rule: never grade on the training set

A model that memorizes its training data can score 100% on it and still be useless — that failure mode is called overfitting. The defense is discipline about data splits:

  • Training set — the examples the model learns from
  • Validation set — used during development to tune choices
  • Test set — touched once, at the end, to estimate real-world performance

This segment also covers loss (the number training tries to minimize) and practical preparation: scaling features so no column dominates, and rebalancing datasets where one class is rare.

content.description: Two intuitive classifiers: vote among your neighbors, or reason with probabilities.
content.problemStatement: Two intuitive classifiers: vote among your neighbors, or reason with probabilities.

contentBlocks.content:
Two ways to classify

K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) barely "learns" at all: to classify a new point, it finds the K most similar training examples and takes a majority vote. Simple, surprisingly strong, and a perfect first model — but the choice of K matters (K=1 overfits; huge K blurs everything).

Naive Bayes instead reasons with probability: using Bayes' theorem, it asks "given these features, which class is most probable?" — assuming (naively) that features are independent. That naive assumption is usually false yet the classifier still works remarkably well, famously for spam filtering.

  • Watch for: distance as "similarity" in KNN
  • Watch for: how both are implemented in a few lines of scikit-learn

content.description: Drawing decision boundaries: probability curves with logistic regression, maximum margins with SVMs.
content.problemStatement: Drawing decision boundaries: probability curves with logistic regression, maximum margins with SVMs.

contentBlocks.content:
Boundaries, not neighborhoods

Logistic regression — despite the name — is a classifier: it fits an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve that outputs a probability between 0 and 1, then thresholds it (usually at 0.5) to decide the class. Because it outputs calibrated probabilities, it is the workhorse of risk scoring in finance and medicine.

Support Vector Machines take a geometric view: among all lines (or hyperplanes) that separate the classes, choose the one with the widest margin to the nearest points — those nearest points are the "support vectors" that give the method its name.

  • Watch for: the sigmoid curve mapping any number into (0, 1)
  • Watch for: why maximizing the margin improves generalization

content.title: Challenge: Compute Model Accuracy
content.question: Given true labels and predicted labels, compute the accuracy as a percentage.
content.description:
You evaluated a classifier. Input format:

line 1: space-separated true labels
line 2: space-separated predicted labels (same length)

Print the accuracy — the fraction of positions where the prediction matches the truth — as a percentage with one decimal place.

Example:

Input:
1 0 1 1 0
1 0 0 1 0

Output:
80.0
content.problemStatement: Read two lines of space-separated labels (true, then predicted) and print the match rate as a percentage with one decimal place. Example: 4 of 5 match → 80.0.

python.body:
true_labels = input().split()
predicted = input().split()

# TODO: count matching positions and print the accuracy
# as a percentage with one decimal place, e.g. 80.0
python.solution:
true_labels = input().split()
predicted = input().split()

matches = sum(1 for t, p in zip(true_labels, predicted) if t == p)
accuracy = matches / len(true_labels) * 100
print(f"{accuracy:.1f}")

testCases.input:
cat dog cat
cat dog cat

content.description: Neurons, layers, activation functions, and backpropagation — then building a real classifier in TensorFlow.
content.problemStatement: Neurons, layers, activation functions, and backpropagation — then building a real classifier in TensorFlow.

contentBlocks.content:
Stacking simple units into deep intelligence

A single artificial neuron is trivial: multiply each input by a weight, add them up, pass the result through an activation function. The power comes from stacking thousands of them in layers — each layer transforming the previous layer's output — and from backpropagation, the algorithm that nudges every weight in the direction that reduces the loss.

  • Watch for: why non-linear activations (ReLU, sigmoid) are what make depth useful
  • Watch for: the training loop — forward pass, loss, backward pass, weight update
  • Watch for: how few lines of TensorFlow it takes to define and train a network

This architecture — scaled up massively — is the same family of models behind modern image recognition and language AI.

content.description: The original ML model: fitting a line, measuring error, and rebuilding it as a neural network.
content.problemStatement: The original ML model: fitting a line, measuring error, and rebuilding it as a neural network.

contentBlocks.content:
Fitting the best line

Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of the inputs: y = w·x + b. "Best" is defined by a loss — most commonly mean squared error (MSE): average the squared differences between predictions and truth. Squaring punishes big misses hard, which is usually what you want.

The elegant finale of this segment: a linear regression is a neural network with one neuron and no activation — so the same TensorFlow machinery trains it. Seeing that connection demystifies deep learning more than anything else in the course.

  • Watch for: residuals — the vertical gaps between points and the fitted line
  • Watch for: MSE as the average of squared residuals (you will implement it next)

content.title: Challenge: Mean Squared Error
content.question: Implement the loss function used to train regression models.
content.description:
Input format:

line 1: space-separated true values
line 2: space-separated predicted values (same length)

Print the mean squared error — the average of squared differences — with two decimal places.

Example:

Input:
3 5 2
2 5 4

Output:
1.67

(differences 1, 0, −2 → squares 1, 0, 4 → mean 5/3 ≈ 1.67)
content.problemStatement: Read two lines of numbers (true, predicted) and print the mean of squared differences with two decimal places. Example: truths 3 5 2, predictions 2 5 4 → 1.67.

python.body:
y_true = [float(v) for v in input().split()]
y_pred = [float(v) for v in input().split()]

# TODO: compute the mean squared error and print it
# with two decimal places, e.g. 1.67
python.solution:
y_true = [float(v) for v in input().split()]
y_pred = [float(v) for v in input().split()]

mse = sum((t - p) ** 2 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / len(y_true)
print(f"{mse:.2f}")

content.description: Finding structure without labels: clustering with K-means and compressing dimensions with PCA.
content.problemStatement: Finding structure without labels: clustering with K-means and compressing dimensions with PCA.

contentBlocks.content:
Learning without answers

Sometimes there are no labels — just data — and the question is "what structure is in here?" K-means answers by clustering: pick K center points, assign every example to its nearest center, move each center to the mean of its members, repeat until stable. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) answers by compression: find the directions along which the data varies most, and project onto them — turning 50 correlated columns into 2 or 3 you can actually plot.

  • Watch for: the assign-then-update loop of K-means converging step by step
  • Watch for: PCA as "the best flattening" of high-dimensional data

content.description: What the math cannot fix: dataset bias, evaluation pitfalls, and the questions to ask before shipping a model.
content.problemStatement: What the math cannot fix: dataset bias, evaluation pitfalls, and the questions to ask before shipping a model.

contentBlocks.content:
The model is only as fair as its data

Every technique in this course optimizes a number — accuracy, MSE, margin. None of them can detect that the number is being optimized on biased data. A hiring model trained on historical decisions learns historical prejudices; a diagnosis model trained mostly on one demographic underperforms on others. Bias in, bias out — at scale, and with a veneer of objectivity.

A practitioner's pre-launch checklist

  • Provenance: where did the training data come from, and who is missing from it?
  • Sliced evaluation: report accuracy per subgroup, not just overall — a 95% average can hide a 60% subgroup
  • Failure cost: a false negative in cancer screening and a false positive in spam filtering have wildly different prices; choose metrics and thresholds accordingly
  • Monitoring: data drifts after deployment — yesterday's accurate model quietly decays
  • Recourse: can an affected person contest an automated decision?

These questions — not the algorithms — are usually what separates AI that helps from AI that harms. Carry them into the final exam and into your work.

questions.title: Challenge: Prediction Log Analyzer
questions.question: Parse a model's prediction log and report per-class correct counts plus overall accuracy.
questions.description:
Each line of input is a log record: true_label,predicted_label. Input ends with a line containing only END.

Print two lines:

  1. correct=X total=Y — the number of correct predictions and total records
  2. accuracy=Z — the accuracy percentage with one decimal place

Example:

Input:
cat,cat
dog,cat
dog,dog
END

Output:
correct=2 total=3
accuracy=66.7
questions.problemStatement: Read lines of true,predicted pairs until END. Print correct=X total=Y then accuracy=Z (one decimal place).

python.body:
# Read lines of "true,predicted" until a line equals END.
# Print:  correct=X total=Y
# Then:   accuracy=Z   (one decimal place)

while True:
    line = input().strip()
    if line == "END":
        break
    # TODO: parse the pair and update your counters
python.solution:
correct = 0
total = 0
while True:
    line = input().strip()
    if line == "END":
        break
    true_label, predicted = line.split(",")
    total += 1
    if true_label == predicted:
        correct += 1
print(f"correct={correct} total={total}")
print(f"accuracy={correct / total * 100:.1f}")
